item.title: When Threat Intelligence Works Against Your SOC: 3 Patterns to Watch For
item.description:
Disclosure: This article was provided by ANY.RUN. The information and analysis presented are based on their research and findings

It wouldn’t be much of an exaggeration to say that threat intelligence, which is supposed to help security teams detect threats earlier, can sometimes have the opposite effect on SOC efficiency.

Poorly selected or implemented threat intelligence sources can introduce new operational challenges and add friction to daily workflows.

Here are three reasons why your threat intelligence might be working against your SOC, and what you can do about it.

Pattern #1. Relying on Threat Data with Limited Coverage and Quality

With SIEM, EDR, and other security systems collecting telemetry, identifying suspicious activity, and helping analysts investigate potential threats, it’s important to remember that these tools primarily provide visibility into your own environment.

External visibility starts with intelligence about malicious infrastructure observed elsewhere. Without it, your SOC risks acting with limited visibility: a threat targets companies in another industry, but you only become aware of it when it reaches your organization.

To break this cycle, you can use external threat intelligence sources. But there’s another problem: their data may be outdated, low-quality, or overlap significantly with what you already have.

How Do You Break This Pattern?

Incorporate threat intelligence derived from real-world malware and phishing investigations across different industries. This helps expand visibility beyond your own environment and provides early warnings about malicious infrastructure observed elsewhere.

For example, ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox can serve as a source of threat data, collecting malicious indicators from real-world malware and phishing analyses across a community of more than 16,000 organizations worldwide.

These indicators are delivered to your SIEM/SOAR/XDR and other systems through Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds), giving SOC teams access to malicious IP addresses, domains, and URLs observed across different industries.

With approximately 99% unique IOCs compared with other threat intelligence sources and a near-zero false positive rate, ANY.RUN TI Feeds help expand coverage without overwhelming analysts with duplicate or irrelevant data.

Expand your SOC’s threat intelligence coverage

Support detection in your existing stack with threat data from 16,000+ SOCs worldwide.

Explore TI Feeds

Pattern #2. Getting Threat Intelligence Too Late

Threat intelligence has a limited window of opportunity. The speed at which intelligence reaches security systems is an important factor in detection effectiveness.

An organization that receives information about malicious infrastructure earlier has a better opportunity to identify matching activity before an incident develops further. It’s all about how quickly new intelligence becomes available to your security stack.

How Do You Break This Pattern?

Continuously updated intelligence that can be delivered into detection systems with minimal delay is the only way to keep up with an ever-changing threat landscape.

ANY.RUN’s research illustrates why this matters. In a study of malicious indicators identified during Interactive Sandbox investigations, approximately 30% of unique malicious IOCs were already present in ANY.RUN TI Feeds before the corresponding investigations began.

This finding does not mean that 30% of all threats can be prevented automatically. Rather, it demonstrates that a meaningful portion of malicious infrastructure observed during investigations may already be known to a broader intelligence network.

When this information is delivered to an organization’s security controls, it creates opportunities to identify matching activity earlier. ANY.RUN TI Feeds support this approach by continuously collecting malicious indicators and instantly updating the feeds for early detection and broader visibility.

Pattern #3. The Distance Between Data and Action: Handling Threat Intelligence Manually

In many SOCs, threat intelligence is distributed across multiple tools and interfaces. Analysts may need to search external platforms, copy indicators between systems, compare results, and manually update detection rules.

Each step may take only a short time. Across hundreds or thousands of alerts, however, this work can consume a substantial share of SOC capacity.

It also creates inconsistencies. Different analysts may use different intelligence sources or follow different enrichment procedures, potentially leading to uneven prioritization and slower investigations.

How Do You Break This Pattern?

Through threat intelligence that integrates directly with existing security infrastructure and supports automated detection and investigation workflows.

ANY.RUN TI Feeds integrate with platforms such as Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender, OpenCTI, Elastic Security, Fortinet, Rapid7, and more through supported connectors, STIX/TAXII, and APIs.

Instead of requiring analysts to retrieve and check indicators manually, TI Feeds deliver malicious IP addresses, domains, and URLs directly into the systems they already use.

This allows SOC teams to build repeatable workflows where incoming indicators are automatically processed and used for threat matching, alert enrichment, and investigation prioritization, depending on the platform and its configuration.

For additional context, SOC teams can also use ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Lookup that adds another layer of investigation, allowing analysts to enrich suspicious indicators with related threat context and hunt for connections to other malicious infrastructure.

ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence solutions connect threat data, automated detection, and deeper investigation, while allowing SOC teams to use the tools that fit their existing workflows.

Making Threat Intelligence Work for Your SOC

For SOC leaders, three priorities matter when choosing threat intelligence sources:

  • Detection coverage: Look for intelligence sources that provide additional visibility into emerging threats, not just more of the same indicators.
  • SOC capacity: Reduce manual intelligence handling through automated delivery and integration with existing workflows.
  • ROI from existing investments: Make better use of SIEM, EDR, SOAR, and other security tools by supplying them with relevant, timely threat intelligence.

By combining independent threat intelligence with automated delivery into existing security systems, organizations can strengthen detection, preserve analyst capacity, and extract more value from their security investments.

Put 99% unique threat intelligence to work in your SOC

Improve threat visibility, increase analyst capacity, and get more value from your security investments.

Integrate TI Feeds

item.title: Researchers Disrupt Massive BADBOX 3.0 Ad Fraud and Proxy Botnet
item.description:
A years-long ad fraud operation targeting cheap, uncertified Android TV boxes, streaming devices and other consumer devices has suffered another major disruption. Digital fraud and bot-defense firm HUMAN reports that its Satori Threat Intelligence team has disrupted BADBOX 3.0, in which the peak volume reached was around 40 billion ad bid requests a day.

This represents over 4% of connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by researchers. Also, it is three times higher than the volume of the previous record-holder, VASTFLUX.

How BADABOX 3.0 Scheme Works

The BADBOX 3.0 campaign started with malware hidden inside cheap Android streaming boxes and tablets, which then connected those infected devices into a large botnet controlled by criminals. This was a coordinated effort involving spreading BADBOX 3.0 malware, playing fake ads, and selling victims’ home internet connections for profit.

The malware ran video ads in a hidden window, which means the device was playing ads even though nothing appeared on the screen, whereas the ad requests seemed to be coming from legitimate streaming apps. This misled advertisers into paying for traffic that was never genuine.

Researchers linked its malware module catalog to Chinese electronics manufacturer TXCZ through device software, domains, server infrastructure and code repositories. They also noted that the malware turned infected devices into residential proxy nodes across 11 networks. This allowed outsiders to use a victim’s home internet connection to route their own traffic while creating an illusion that it was coming from an ordinary household and conceal their actual location.

BADBOX keeps coming back

Hackread.com first reported on BADBOX in October 2023 when researchers at HUMAN found backdoors on cheap Android TV boxes and tablets. The malware was already installed before the devices reached buyers, leaving them compromised from the moment they were switched on. HUMAN found more than 74,000 infected devices while the PEACHPIT component was being used to commit ad fraud.

By July 2025, BADBOX had returned on a much larger scale with BADBOX 2.0 infecting more than 10 million devices across 222 countries and territories. It came with a new backdoor, BB2DOOR, which gave operators ways to commit click fraud, manipulate ads and sell access to victims’ internet connections. The campaign led to a disruption effort involving Google and other partners.

BADBOX 3.0 is different from the previous versions as instead of keeping all its malware in one place, it fetches new modules from public code repositories via a C2 server. It also hosts backup copies on other platforms and content delivery networks (CDNs) in case files get removed. That allows operators to replace malware and keep devices working for them. Some of the fake ad traffic was also created without an infected device, using bogus server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests (called SSAI spoofing).

Researchers also believe IpMoYu, a residential proxy network exposed during the BADBOX 2.0 investigation, has returned as PXYEDGE. The new service advertised around 200,000 nodes, while monitoring recorded as many as 340,000 unique connections across its services.

The latest disruption is a huge blow, but BADBOX’s history offers little reason to assume its operators will stop here. We’ve seen the operation getting disrupted, then returning, the infrastructure moving, and the fraud evolving. Cheap devices with questionable software and little security oversight remain an easy way back in.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Free vs. Paid Security Tools: Where Free Options Fall Short
item.description:
Many free security tools offer solid protection, helping companies detect and block threats and keep daily operations secure. For small businesses, startups, and independent companies with limited IT budgets, these tools are a practical way to keep cybersecurity costs under control without leaving gaps in protection.

Identifying the differences between free cybersecurity tools and paid software may prove to be very useful for business people to make informed decisions about securing their systems, employees, and data.

Free Tools Cover Prevention Better Than Most Owners Think 

This is an era of advanced free cybersecurity tools. New firms no longer need to pay for sophisticated software to protect themselves from potential threats. However, many free applications can offer multiple security tools such as:

  • Antivirus Software: This software helps identify and detect known viruses and isolate and remove malware.
  • Password Managers: For storing employee/user login information and ensuring passwords are not reused.
  • Firewalls: These can be used for monitoring traffic to the network and controlling access to it.
  • Browser security extension: Helps users avoid accessing harmful websites and informs the user regarding any suspicious links on the site.
  • The other kinds of security methods utilized by companies are multi-factor authentication.

Using free software for small business cybersecurity can lead to increased security. There are various free software options for account protection and secure communications.

The Gaps Show Up After the Alert, Not Before It 

Prevention is merely a tactic within cybersecurity. If it circumvents any of these defenses, businesses must grasp what is going on, the seriousness of the incident, and what steps will be taken to minimize the effects. Common limitations include:

  • One-way investigation: Limited investigations that do not attempt to detail how an attacker got in or which systems have been impacted can be performed with free software.
  • No fixed response (business) team: The business team may find themselves in a situation where they are tasked with taking action without technical expertise.
  • No continuous monitoring: There are free solutions that do not provide continuous monitoring, so you have to check alerts yourself.
  • Not enough reporting: The detailed history of incidents and security analytics/compliance reports are only available through paid subscriptions.

The FBI 2025 Internet Crime Report stated that the Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million complaints, with losses on the verge of $21 billion. That’s up from a year ago when that figure was $16.6 billion.

What You’re Paying For Is Response Time 

In addition, paid cybersecurity services may offer further security measures such as:

  • Continuous security monitoring.
  • Vulnerability assessments.
  • Professional incident response.
  • Detailed security reporting.
  • Technical and recovery assistance.
  • Special training in advanced threat detection and investigation.

Think about the impact of an employee opening an email attachment with a link that leads to malicious content. Suspicious activity may be caught by a simple free program, and an alert may be sent. But a more full-blown commercial offering may make a difference:

  • Determine the source of the threat.
  • Segment the device that is affected.
  • Look into possible compromise of other systems.
  • Identify if information is sensitive and if it has been released.
  • Help with recovery and help ensure that similar incidents never happen again.

Rapid response is critical because of the rapid growth that cyber incidents can experience. Cyber providers such as Cyber Husky can help by offering expertise without the burden of an in-house security team. 

Decide Control by Control, Not Tool by Tool 

It is wrong to assume that all free tools must go to make way for one paid tool, but it is right to ascertain your personal security requirements and know where additional protection will cost the company more. The following comparison may be helpful to begin:

A small business that manages relatively limited amounts of sensitive data might be OK accepting free software for some of its functions. For smaller businesses that hold customer records, financial data, or business-sensitive information, though, more extensive small business cybersecurity measures might be required. 

Conclusion 

Free cybersecurity products play a key part in business security nowadays. They provide inexpensive protection, which may assist you in creating a certain level of protection without having to create an expensive subscription. However, prevention is not the only solution. 

Organizations need to be capable of investigating any suspicious activities, responding to them, and recovering from them without causing too much disruption. If you do not know how vulnerable your current security protection system is, you can use that information to get a professional security evaluation. 

(Featured Image via Magnific)

item.title: Researchers Take Over Five US Treasury Subdomains for About $3 Each
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers at Intruder took control of five US Treasury subdomains for about $3 each by claiming Amazon Web Services (AWS) IP addresses that the subdomains still pointed to.

The researchers demonstrated that they could publish their own content on the affected addresses. Intruder did not report access to Treasury’s internal systems or theft of government data.

How old DNS records left the subdomains exposed

When an organisation retires a cloud server, its DNS records can still direct visitors to the server’s old IP address. If the cloud provider assigns that address to another customer, the new holder can serve content under the original subdomain. That leftover entry is known as a dangling DNS record.

In its research report, shared with Hackread.com, Intruder said it tested whether AWS Elastic IP addresses matched live DNS records. Over 48 hours, the researchers checked about 450,000 unique IP addresses and found 28 matches. Nearly half belonged to government organisations.

Five US Treasury subdomains pointed to addresses Intruder controlled:

  1. ftp.treasury.gov
  2. pcp.treasury.gov
  3. ww5.treasury.gov
  4. rdgw.treasury.gov
  5. irssearch.treasury.gov

Someone who gains control of a government subdomain could host a phishing page on a genuine .gov address and obtain a valid HTTPS certificate. Intruder also warned that older automated systems could still send credentials to a retired address, and that cookies configured to be shared with subdomains could be exposed. The report described these as risks and did not document credential or cookie theft.

AWS says customers are responsible for removing old DNS records

AWS blocked Intruder’s account from claiming or using Elastic IP addresses after 48 hours of testing. The researchers said they were still able to transfer addresses they had already claimed to another account within the same AWS organisation.

Intruder asked AWS to limit monthly IP allocations and apply restrictions to entire organisations. According to Intruder, AWS said on November 17 that it had no plans to make those changes and maintained that customers were responsible for removing obsolete DNS records.

Intruder said it notified the organisations affected by all 28 findings and that the DNS records were fixed. Its test covered 0.56% of AWS’s published EC2 IPv4 address space. For organisations retiring cloud services, the practical step is to remove or update the DNS records before releasing the addresses they point to.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Open database exposed 2 billion credential records, including session tokens
item.description:
A database containing roughly 2 billion credentials was accessible online without a password or encryption, allowing anyone who came across it easy access to a massive data trove.

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered the database, describing it as a suspected data breach of a criminal marketplace or aggregation operation possibly affecting millions of individuals, businesses, organizations, and government accounts. The findings were published by ExpressVPN and shared with Hackread.com.

A Massive Credential Collection Exposed

Fowler dubs it the largest credential collection he has encountered in his career so far. It is at least 13 times larger than another exposure of 149 million logins he had reported earlier this year. But this time the exposed records aren’t just limited to usernames and passwords- the database contained cookies, session tokens, and other stolen information as well.

As stated by the researcher, he found around 8,471 folders, among which were plaintext credentials and account information (some even arranged by country codes like US, UK, FR, DE, ES, and MX).

Separately, Fowler found 400,000 documents probably collected by more advanced infostealer malware. These files mainly contained browser data, clipboard contents, system information, and cryptocurrency-related details.

Thousands of credentials associated with Tor .onion services were also found. These include private forums, marketplaces, and other services accessible through the Tor network. Moreover, domain-based searches returned more than 608 million Gmail records, 61.4 million entries linked to .gov domains, and nearly 50 million .org records. Fowler also reported finding records from some of the world’s widely used platforms, including:

  • X: 32.8 million
  • Facebook: 88 million
  • Roblox: 41.7 million
  • Amazon: 36.6 million
  • Instagram: 31 million
  • Discord: 20.7 million
  • Google Services: 114.2 million
  • OpenAI and ChatGPT combined: over 2.2 million

In the blog post, Fowler clarified that these are database matches and not confirmed victims or active accounts and that the records could be duplicated or used by the same person across multiple services. The hosting provider restricted access several days after Fowler reported it.

Potential Dangers of this Exposure

Fowler suspects a criminal marketplace was breached; the database owner’s identity is still unclear. Some files contained Telegram branding and advertisements for geo-targeted email lists, but Fowler could not establish whether the server belonged to a criminal data broker, reseller, or legitimate research operation.

A database containing roughly 2 billion credentials was accessible online without a password or encryption, allowing anyone who came across it easy access to a massive data trove.

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered the database, describing it as a suspected data breach of a criminal marketplace or aggregation operation possibly affecting millions of individuals, businesses, organizations, and government accounts. The findings were published by ExpressVPN and shared with Hackread.com.

A Massive Credential Collection Exposed

Fowler dubs it the largest credential collection he has encountered in his career so far. It is at least 13 times larger than another exposure of 149 million logins he had reported earlier this year. But this time the exposed records aren’t just limited to usernames and passwords- the database contained cookies, session tokens, and other stolen information as well.

As stated by the researcher, he found around 8,471 folders, among which were plaintext credentials and account information (some even arranged by country codes like US, UK, FR, DE, ES, and MX).

Separately, Fowler found 400,000 documents probably collected by more advanced infostealer malware. These files mainly contained browser data, clipboard contents, system information, and cryptocurrency-related details.

Thousands of credentials associated with Tor .onion services were also found. These include private forums, marketplaces, and other services accessible through the Tor network. Moreover, domain-based searches returned more than 608 million Gmail records, 61.4 million entries linked to .gov domains, and nearly 50 million .org records.   • Facebook: 88 million
  • Roblox: 41.7 million
  • Amazon: 36.6 million
  • Instagram: 31 million
  • Discord: 20.7 million
  • Google Services: 114.2 million
  • OpenAI and ChatGPT combined: over 2.2 million

item.title: FBI Helps Free Over 2,200 Trafficking Victims in Global Scam Crackdown
item.description:
The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced charges, convictions, sentences, extraditions and other legal actions against more than 800 defendants across 400 cases involving scams and online fraud since March. The cases cover a range of schemes, from cryptocurrency investment fraud and impersonation scams to fraudulent call centers.

Announced on November 24 in a press release, the action also involved overseas raids, extraditions and efforts to recover money stolen from victims. US authorities worked alongside law enforcement in more than 10 countries in this effort.

The crackdown follows President Trump’s March 6 Executive Order 14390, which directed federal agencies to intensify efforts against online fraud.

Scam compounds, stolen funds and forced labor

As part of the crackdown, the FBI is working to dismantle scam networks through Operation Blackout- its global initiative to identify and dismantle scam compounds and disrupt the criminal networks behind them. The bureau reportedly has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices, and helped dismantle over 29 scam compounds across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East.

This is an important part of the crackdown because the operation helped free and repatriate more than 2,200 people who were trafficked into the compounds and forced to carry out scams. Hackread.com has reported on fraud operations that rely on people who themselves are victims of trafficking.

In April, an investigation linked a Cambodian scam compound to an Android banking trojan targeting users in 21 countries, showing that these facilities can support more than just online investment fraud.

US agencies tackle fraud at home

Several agencies reported their own enforcement results. Homeland Security Investigations made more than 300 arrests and reported over $120 million in illicit proceeds seized, restrained, frozen or recovered. The Secret Service, meanwhile, restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds, disrupted 1,780 scam-related domains and investigated over 1,540 business email compromise incidents.

The Securities and Exchange Commission also filed actions against 39 entities accused of using false adviser registration filings to appear legitimate and attract investors. Meanwhile, the Federal Communications Commission approved prison phone-jamming rules to deal with scams carried out via smuggled mobile phones.

In Georgia, inmates allegedly used contraband phones to impersonate court officials, telling victims into that they had missed jury duty and faced arrest unless they paid a fake fine. Fourteen people were charged in these schemes, while another 17 faced charges related to smuggling phones into prisons.

The cases show how scammers keep exploiting everything from online platforms and investment schemes to phone calls. Despite the crackdown, the scale of the problem remains high, with Gallup estimating Americans lost $68 billion to scams in 2025 and 10% of US adults experiencing a scam directly or through someone in their household.

Expert’s Commentary

Dave Hayes, Vice President of Product at cybersecurity company FusionAuth, shared his thoughts with Hackread.com on why fraudsters can bypass bank security checks by manipulating victims into making payments themselves, and what banks could do to spot suspicious transactions.

“In most of the scams in this crackdown, the bank checked the right person, because the victim logged in on their own phone and sent the money themselves. Nobody checked the caller who was posing as a court or a bank and telling them to do it. The scammer has no authority over the account, so they work through the one person who does.

“When we decide whether to trust a login, a new device is usually just a new phone, but a new device an hour after a password change is a reason to ask for more proof. A phone call can be checked the same way. Watch for a number you don’t know, pressure to pay today, a request to move money somewhere new, and a story that can’t be true, like a court that takes fines at a crypto kiosk.”

“If two of those show up on one call, hang up and call them back on a number you look up yourself. Banks should run that check on the payment, even after the login passes. A first transfer to a crypto exchange, for more than the customer has ever sent anywhere, should be held until the bank has spoken to them.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: AI Can Write Code. Engineers Still Have to Decide What Ships
item.description:
US software development job postings on Indeed rose nearly 15% from late February 2025 through the period covered by its July 2026 analysis, while overall US job postings fell 7%. Senior roles accounted for 71% of the increase in software development postings between May 2025 and May 2026, according to Indeed Hiring Lab. Roles with AI in the job title accounted for 37% of the increase over that same year.

Software development postings were still about 27.5% below their pre-pandemic level. The figures show where demand has returned on Indeed, but they don’t tell us how many people companies hired or whether AI caused the rebound.

Alejandro Gomez, founder and CEO of Zaga, which places engineers from Latin America in US product teams, said his clients now expect more from the engineers they hire. “AI didn’t reduce our clients’ appetite for engineers. It raised their standard for them,” he said.

The rebound in postings has favoured senior roles

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that software developer employment will grow 15.8% between 2024 and 2034, adding 267,700 jobs. That is a forecast for the profession; it does not measure how many jobs AI has already changed or replaced.

The picture looks different for people entering the workforce. In an August 2026 update, Stanford Digital Economy Lab researchers estimated that employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in occupations highly exposed to AI was 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with employment among less-exposed workers of the same age. Experienced workers showed no comparable gap. The study covers several occupations, including software development, and does not establish AI as the sole cause.

Developers trust AI output when they can check it

In Stack Overflow’s 2026 Developer Survey, 48% of respondents to the trust question said they trusted AI output when they could easily verify it. About 7% said they trusted it for many tasks, including important work decisions.

Google’s 2025 DORA report found that 90% of the technology professionals it surveyed used AI at work, while 30% reported little or no trust in AI-generated code. The report found that AI tended to magnify a team’s existing strengths and weaknesses. If a team already struggles to review and test changes, generating more code gives it more work to check.

What AI fluency looks like on an engineering team

An engineer who uses AI well can explain why a proposed change belongs in the codebase, test what happens when inputs are missing or unexpected, and spot issues such as a permission check the generated code left out. The engineer also needs to know when to discard a suggestion and write the change from scratch.

Employers are asking for both technical and communication skills. ManpowerGroup’s Q4 2026 Experis Tech Talent Outlook found that employers were prioritising AI capabilities alongside the skills needed to work with others. In an engineering team, those skills show up when someone can explain what they tested, what remains uncertain and why a change is ready to release.

A practical interview exercise is to give candidates a short piece of AI-generated code and ask what they would test, what they would change and whether they would ship it. Pay attention to the evidence they ask for before they say yes.

(Photo by Growtika on Unsplash)

item.title: 1Password Says Hacker Copied Customer Account Data, Vaults Unaffected
item.description:
Password manager 1Password said on November 25 that a hacker copied account information belonging to some customers, including names and email addresses used to sign in. The company said the hacker did not access customer vaults, the passwords and other items stored in them, or the encryption keys that protect them. It did not say how many customers were affected.

1Password said in its incident notice that it began investigating on November 19 after finding signs that someone had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker used the account to push malicious code to internal services and copy customer records.

The unknown attackers also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the system 1Password uses to build and deploy software. The company said the source code contained no customer secrets.

Some invitation and recovery links were affected

Along with names and email addresses, the copied records included account and user IDs, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys and other account metadata. The records also contained tokens from some emailed links used to invite users, set up accounts or recover access. 1Password said in its blog post that it notified the small number of users whose provisioning or recovery tokens were affected.

Anyone holding one of those tokens would still need to sign in through the organisation’s single sign-on system or enter a verification code sent to the registered email address, 1Password said. The company found no evidence that the exposed tokens were used to take over accounts and changed the verification codes from six digits to ten letters and numbers. The public keys in the copied records are separate from the keys that protect customer vaults.

1Password says customers do not need to change their passwords

1Password disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token and restored clean versions of the affected service. It also replaced or revoked internal credentials that could have been exposed and brought in independent cybersecurity experts to review its response. The company said its apps and services were operating normally.

Customers do not need to change their passwords or update their accounts because of the incident, 1Password said. It advised treating unexpected invitations and account recovery messages with caution. If one arrives, open 1Password directly to check it. The company says it will never contact customers to ask for their account password or Secret Key.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Hackers used Hugging Face’s AI site builder to create fake Microsoft login pages
item.description:
Building fake login pages for renowned services like Microsoft or PayPal doesn’t require much efforts for cybercriminals anymore, reports cybersecurity firm Aikido. In its latest research blog shared with Hackread.com, the company explained details of a phishing campaign in which attackers used Hugging Face’s AI website builder to create phishing pages and published them through its hosting service called Hugging Face Spaces.

Aikido researcher Hunter Schwartz discovered this fraud. He found 42 pages impersonating 28 brands. Schwartz started investigating after a malware scan flagged a suspicious Jupyter notebook containing a hidden script displaying a fake Hugging Face login. Though the notebook was labelled as a security test, it led Schwartz to search for more phishing pages on the platform.

Attackers Told the AI What to Build

Among the 42 pages, Schwartz found that 29 were made using Hugging Face’s AI website builder called DeepSite. This builder generates and publishes websites from written prompts, and this feature allowed attackers to build phishing pages without writing code.

Digging deeper, Schwartz found prompts instructing DeepSite to copy login pages, send stolen details to Telegram, and redirect victims to genuine websites after collecting their information. A fake Microsoft login page that he analyzed was built through 15 commits, 14 of which were made within 90 minutes on October 25, 2025.

According to Aikido’s blog post, some operators told the AI to hide pages from Google and Bing crawlers, headless browsers, curl, and wget, so that automated tools cannot inspect them, while some asked it to reject the first password entered to force victims to type their credentials again.

The company found no sign that the operators wrote the code themselves. Instead, commit histories showed them instructing the AI and asking it to make changes.

Stolen Data and Pages That Stayed Online

Until 16 October, 34 of these pages were live while 8 were paused, Aikido observed. Also, researchers noted that 25 sent stolen data to Telegram bots, 11 used Discord webhooks, and 6 relied on form services. Not all the pages asked for passwords only, though.

The collected data depended on the target, such as, some pages collected one-time codes, payment card details, banking transaction passwords, phone numbers, dates of birth, and IP addresses whereas some redirected victims to the real website after collecting their information, making the phishing attempt less obvious.

Another important discovery was that 23 of these pages had been published more than a year earlier with the oldest dating back to April 26, 2025. However, their publication dates do not confirm how long they remained continuously active and Aikido also could not establish how many people visited the pages or entered their details.

Researchers reported all 42 pages to Hugging Face on October 16, and all were paused or were no longer publicly accessible by October 29.

Aikido researchers suggest that blocking all `hf.space` links isn’t a practical fix as legitimate apps use them too so a better protection strategy would be checking DNS, proxy, and email logs for suspicious links.

This is not the first time Hugging Face has been abused. In July, Hackread.com reported on AI agents exploiting vulnerabilities and exposed credentials to access parts of the platform’s production infrastructure. That incident involved access to internal systems, while the latest one used Hugging Face’s public hosting features to steal credentials. The methods were different, but both involved attackers exploiting the platform.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: 905,672 Characters Under Black Rectangles: Why a Qualified Signature Can’t Vouch for a GDPR Export
item.description:
A qualified electronic signature proves who sent a PDF and that nobody altered it afterwards. It proves nothing about whether the redactions removed anything, whether the export is complete, or how the visible sample was chosen.

Drawing a black box over text in a PDF is not redaction. Security engineers have said this for two decades, usually after a court filing or government release spills its entire text layer to anyone who selects all and pastes. The mistake persists anyway. In European privacy compliance, it now arrives with a stronger credential attached: the qualified electronic signature.

Under EU law, a qualified electronic signature (QES) has the same legal effect as a handwritten one. When a data controller, or counsel acting for it, answers an Article 15 GDPR access request with a QES-signed document, the recipient is expected to accept the file as complete, properly sanitized and checked.

That expectation conflates two separate questions. A signature binds an identity to a sequence of bytes and shows that those bytes have not changed since signing. It cannot show that the text under a black rectangle was deleted. It cannot show that a missing category of data was lawfully withheld. It cannot even show that the signer opened the attachment.

Claim Versus Bytes: An 830-Page Export

The open-source TgWitness project has published a documented zero-trust GDPR export case study that tests institutional assurances directly against file contents. Every figure in it is tied to published SHA-256 hashes and can be reproduced offline. That makes the attachment at its center (Anlage 1, 830 pages) a clean specimen of how a conventional Article 15 production goes wrong.

Start with the redactions. Aspose.PDF for .NET 20.8 generated the PDF and masked it with 1,044 black rectangles. The cover correspondence cited protection of third-party rights as the reason for withholding. A stock text extractor such as pdftotext disagrees: 905,672 characters sit intact beneath the overlays.

Those characters are not filler. They include the account login names and complaint descriptions of more than 1,800 unrelated third-party users. A process justified by third-party privacy delivered third-party personal data straight to the requester.

Then the metadata. According to the correspondence, the full statutory month was needed because records had to be cleaned by hand. Whatever review came before the export, the file itself was created and last modified within 36 seconds, from 19:58:05 to 19:58:41.

What a Failed Redaction Reveals About Selection

When a controller withholds 97 percent of a table, outsiders normally have no way to audit how the visible rows were chosen. Here the surviving text layer makes that audit possible. The 50 complaint descriptions left readable can be set against the 1,944 hidden under rectangles (1,995 rows in total, one of them empty).

Across all 1,995 rows, “Offensive Profile” appears 1,148 times (57.5 percent) and “Suspected Hijacker” 312 times (15.6 percent). Among the 50 readable rows, 43 (86 percent) are labelled “Suspected Hijacker.” The number labelled “Offensive Profile” is zero.

Draw 50 rows at random from that pool and the hypergeometric probability of getting 43 or more from the 15.6 percent category is roughly 6.2 × 10-29. Whatever picked the visible sample, it was not chance.

The sample’s content has problems of its own. Several of the readable complaints, dated August 2025, allege that an account was suddenly stolen or had its password changed overnight. The same PDF contradicts them. Its login history ends in May 2025, and the security history on page 830 records the last password change in July 2024. That page was itself placed under a black rectangle.

A qualified signature catches none of this. The signature validates, the SHA-256 digest matches and the container is intact. The contents are not.

Where Trust-Based Compliance Fails

Article 15 exists to give data subjects verifiable access to their own data, not a summary curated by whoever holds the server logs. In disputes over valuable accounts, payments or platform enforcement, the trust-only model fails every party at the table.

Controllers that substitute visual overlays for byte-level removal turn a routine access request into a reportable breach of third-party data. Requesters cannot tell whether absent categories, such as payment histories, support tickets, or internal review records, were withheld on a valid legal basis or simply left out. Regulators and courts inherit disputes in which neither side can prove what the original export contained without rerunning the investigation from scratch.

A black box solves none of these problems. Neither does a signature on the cover letter.

Verify the File, Not the Sender

The fix requires no new legislation and no exotic cryptography. Two standard primitives are enough, arranged so that no party has to be taken at its word.

The first is physical removal backed by per-field salted commitments. Any value withheld from the requester, a third-party username, for instance, is stripped from the requester’s copy before the document is generated.

In its place goes a signed commitment, c = SHA-256(salt || value), computed with a fresh 16-byte random salt for each field. The salt defeats dictionary attacks. Without it, anyone could hash a list of common usernames or short words and match the result. The signature binds the controller to the hidden value, so it cannot be quietly altered or swapped later.

The second is a sealed envelope addressed to an independent authority. The original values and their salts are encrypted to the public key of the competent supervisory authority or court, using OpenPGP or a hybrid scheme such as RSA-OAEP-256 key wrapping with AES-256-GCM.

A signed manifest accompanies both files. It names every included category, counts every withheld record and states the exact filtering rule applied.

If the requester disputes an omission, nobody has to trust anybody. The authority decrypts the envelope with its private key, recomputes SHA-256 (salt || value) for each withheld field and compares the output with the signed commitments. One altered byte breaks the hash. One dropped record breaks the manifest count.

The receiving infrastructure already exists. Germany’s Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) and several state data protection authorities publish OpenPGP keys for encrypted submissions. German courts routinely accept end-to-end encrypted filings through EGVP over OSCI.

The Bottom Line

An automated PDF export dotted with black rectangles is not privacy protection. It is a plaintext leak waiting for a single command. Until legal and engineering teams treat sender authentication and content verification as separate checks, qualified signatures will keep vouching for broken files. In digital evidence, the title on page one proves very little. What counts is a check that anyone can repeat.
